newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: U.S. security man "invited" to leave Colombia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. security man "invited" to leave Colombia.

text.p: A U.S. security consultant was ordered to leave Colombia because he entered the country without a proper visa and was using its chronic problems with kidnapping to drum up new business, officials said on Monday.

Ruben Dario Ramirez, head of the government's special anti-kidnapping office, said members of the state security police had "invited" the consultant with Kroll Associates Ltd. to leave the country within 72 hours last Friday.
"He entered the country on a tourist card," Ramirez told Reuters, adding that Kroll had angered the government by claiming that 4,000 kidnapping cases occurred in Colombia last year alone.
The consultant, who Ramirez did not name, had been using the grossly exaggerated statistic as a "marketing tool," he said.

Richard McCormick, senior managing director of Kroll Associates, conceded in a telephone interview from Miami that one of their consultants had left Colombia on Saturday after being asked to do so by the security police.

"We screwed up," McCormick said, adding that the man, who he would not identify, entered the country without a business or work visa. He said, however, that this was a farily common practice among people travelling in and out of Colombia to do security consulting work.

McCormick added that statistics on abduction cases in Colombia, which has the world's highest kidnapping rate, were "all across the board" but that Kroll regretted including the 4,000 figure in an annual report.
"That 4,000 thing was very embarrassing for the government," he said, adding Kroll in the future would publish nothing but official statistics on crime in Colombia.
According to the National Police, the number of abductions in Colombia increased 39 percent last year to 1,608. Ramirez said the actual number was closer to 970.
"Colombia in general, compared to other countries, is trying to deal with the kidnap problem," McCormick said. He added, however, that it was a problem that often seemed insurmountable.
